68 Συμφορὰ γὰρ ἐπίμονος γεροντικὴν ἀσθένειαν ἐμποιεῖ. 69 Οὐ γὰρ ἀφῆκέ με
διαφυγεῖν τὰ δεινὰ πανταχόθεν πολιορκού μενον. λέγοι δ' ἂν ἴσως καὶ τὸ
περιβληθὲν τῇ πόλει τεῖχος πολέ μιον. τὴν αὐτὴν δὲ τῷ ∆αβὶδ ἀφῆκε φωνὴν
εἰρηκότι· «ἐκάθισάν με ἐν σκοτεινοῖς ὡς νεκροὺς αἰῶνος». τοῦτο δὲ διὰ τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν
πολε μίων εἱρκτάς, ἅμα δὲ καὶ διὰ τὰς ἐκ θεοῦ συμφοράς· ψυχῆς γὰρ σκότος οἱ
πειρασμοί. ἰδικῶς δὲ «Ἱερεμίαν καὶ εἰς τὸν καταρράκτην ἐνέβαλεν ὁ Πασχώρ»,
σκοτεινὸν ὄντα καὶ ἀφεγγῆ, ὁποῖον ἦν καὶ τῷ ∆αβὶδ τὸ σπήλαιον ἐν ᾧ παρὰ Σαοὺλ
ἀπεκρύπτετο. δύναιντο δὲ καὶ εἰς Χριστὸν οἱ δύο Θρῆνοι λαμβάνεσθαι, οὗ τύπος ἦν
Ἱερεμίας τοσαῦτα παρὰ Ἰουδαίων πεπονθότος καὶ τέλος τάφῳ παραδοθέντος. 70
Ἀφύκτοις με κακοῖς περιβέβληκεν, ἐπιθεὶς τῷ τραχήλῳ μου λαὸν ἀπηνῆ καὶ
παραπικραίνοντα καὶ μεῖζον ἢ κατ' ἐμὲ φορτίον. οὐκ εἰσηκούσθην δὲ κουφισθῆναι
πολλάκις εὐξάμενος · εἰσακου σθῆναι γὰρ τοὺς ἁγίους ἔσθ' ὅτε κωλύει τ
pass_a_gloss: Persistent sorrow brings on a frailty like that of the aged. He would not let me flee the horrors encircling me on all sides, besieging me. One might say the city’s imposed wall is a heavy, prolonged load. Yet he gave me the same voice David had when he cried, “You have set me in darkness like the dead of old.” This comes from the enemy’s siege works and also from God’s afflictions, for soul-trials are darkness. Notably, Jeremiah was thrown by Pashhur into the dark, lightless cistern, like the cave where David hid from Saul. These two laments may also apply to Christ, whose figure was Jeremiah, who endured much from the Jews and ended in the tomb. He has wrapped me in bitter things, laying on my neck a harsh, aggravating people, a burden greater than my due. Though I often prayed for ease, I was not answered; for even saints’ prayers are sometimes blocked by events. One might compare this to the yoke and iron chains, which God replaced the wooden ones he ordered, and placed on me; for it is said and written that he weighed down the bronze of my neck. He shut my prayer and told me, “Do not pray about them; for I will not hear you.” Having often been moved to act, I was not allowed to quit the burden. For he said, “I will not speak the Lord’s name,” and he was driven on as if by fire. He also blocks the paths of sinners, not permitting them to sin twelve times. The prophet is not like those who feasted in assembly, for he says he did not sit among revelers. All his arrows struck me, wounding my longing and blocking my will. Scripture calls kidneys the seat of desire, arrows the weapons. They drove me on as a false singer, making me chant. Approaching, he declared: "I sat alone, filled with bitterness," and added: one interceded for them, others schemed, yet the service could not be refused. Thus he endured their blows and felt their pain, while himself growing proud and irreverent beneath them. He speaks of each tooth-grind against the cheek as a vote, a count, or a hard stone. He cites David: "I ate my bread with ashes," meaning no joy in food, only sorrow from distress. So my soul knew no rest, torn inside by conflict, outside by noise. Expecting no good, I silenced Job’s cries: "Mercy left me; my hope is from the Lord." No victory over the surrounding terrors was possible. Since he is good to all, he asks for our patience. The soul that seeks him finds good in the seeking, which waits undisturbed till mercy replies, unmoved till the Lord’s salvation appears, to hope in another. Maybe he will be still, saying he does not fuss overly with providence’s decrees. Do not ignore the Lord even if unaware; His yoke is easy, burden light. If none agree with Him, do not follow; if alone, hold fast to the decided. The Lord settles the solitary in a home—David says so—and declares himself alone until passing, meaning one who gains philanthropy’s trial. He humbles Himself: "I am dust and ashes," if truly man; the unashamed hope fills Him, as "My soul clings to the dust." This fits captives singing Psalm 73: "Why, God, cast us off forever? Your wrath smokes against Your flock?" Yet the Lord will not cast off forever nor rage to the end. He tells the penitent: "Let your voice stop weeping, eyes dry." Thus we learn: the Lord did not cause nor is He the reason the earth’s bound are humbled by sin, nor does He bend human judgment against God; He loves justice and straightness, nor does He condemn the worthy. For He says opposites cannot come from His mouth—good and evil. No good tree yields bad fruit, no bad tree...
pass_b_english:
For sorrow, when it persists, induces a weakness akin to old age. For he did not allow me to escape the terrors that surround me on every side, besieging me. One might perhaps also say that the wall cast upon the city is a long, laborious burden. Yet he left me the same voice that David once uttered, saying: “He has made me sit in darkness as those who are dead of the age.” This is due both to the siege works raised against me from all sides and simultaneously to the afflictions that come from God; for the trials of the soul are darkness. Specifically, “Jeremiah was cast by Pashhur into the cistern,” a place dark and lightless, just as the cave in which David hid from Saul was dark. These two laments could also be understood as referring to Christ, of whom Jeremiah was a type, having suffered so much at the hands of the Jews and ultimately being handed over to the grave. He has clothed me in bitter things, placing upon my neck a people that is cruel and provoking, a burden heavier than what is due to me. Though I often prayed for relief, my cries were not heard; for even the prayers of the saints are sometimes hindered by circumstances. One might also liken this to the yoke and the iron chains, which God substituted for the wooden ones he had commanded, and they were placed upon me; for it is reported, and even written, that he weighed down the bronze of my neck. Indeed, he blocked my prayer and said to me: “Do not pray concerning them; for I will not hear you.” Moreover, having often been stirred to action, I was not permitted to withdraw from the burden. For he declared: “I will not name the name of the Lord,” and he was driven on as though by fire. He also obstructs the ways of the sinners, not allowing them to sin twelve times.

But such is not the prophet, who indeed says: "I did not sit in the council of those who revel." He declares that every arrow of his has been spent against me, piercing my desire and refusing to let me act as I wish. For in the Scripture, the kidneys represent the faculty of desire, and the arrows are the missiles. Moreover, they have driven me onward as a liar, having made me sing a song. And having come upon me, he said: "I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness," and what follows: the one indeed prayed for them, while the others plotted against them; yet nevertheless, the ministry was not to be declined. Thus, he prevailed and suffered all things at their hands, and he sympathized with them in their suffering, while he himself grew arrogant beneath them, acting impiously. He says, either by vote or by number, that for each tooth of the one gnashing against the cheek, there is either a hard stone. And concerning David, he says: "I ate my bread with ashes," meaning that he did not take bread with pleasure, but under affliction. Therefore, the soul could not be in peace, being troubled within and still seeing disturbances from without, and within, battles. Hence, hoping for nothing good, I have dismissed the voices of Job: "Mercy has departed from me, and my hope is from the Lord." For it was not possible to overcome the dreadful things that surround. For being good toward all, he demands our endurance. For the soul that seeks him, it is good to seek, which waits without being disturbed, until mercy answers it, and does not waver, until the saving appearance of the Lord is revealed, so that one may hope in another. Perhaps, too, he will be silent, saying that he does not meddle excessively in the providence of judgments.

It is therefore necessary, even if we are ignorant, not to neglect the Lord. For "His yoke is easy and His burden is light." Even if no one agrees with Him on this matter, we must not follow the crowd, but even if we are left alone in this stance, we must persevere and be firmly rooted in what has been decided. For the Lord says, as David declares, "He makes the solitary dwell in a house," and "I am alone until I pass over," clearly referring to those who attain the trials of philanthropy. For He humbles Himself by saying, "I am dust and ashes," if indeed He is truly a man, and the hope that does not shame is filled within Him, just as it is written, "My soul clings to the dust." This also applies to those in captivity who speak the words of the seventy-third Psalm: "Why, O God, have You cast us off forever? Why does Your anger smoke against the sheep of Your pasture?" Yet in agreement with this, it is said, "The Lord will not cast off forever, nor will He be angry to the end." And He will say to the one who has turned to worthiness: "Let your voice cease from weeping, and your eyes from tears." Through these things we learn that the Lord did not say, nor is He the cause of the humiliation of the earth's prisoners under sin, nor does He incline human judgments against God; for the Lord loves justice and uprightness, and He does not even condemn the worthy man. For He says, it is impossible for opposites to proceed from the mouth of the Lord—both good and evil. For neither does a good tree produce bad fruit, nor does a bad tree...
